actionThatDiffers: You open the one pane you actually want instead of cycling three to find it; saves seconds, changes no decision.
why: Claude Code already generates session titles and cwd is in ps/tmux, so a pane sweep yields an adequate one-line identity today (rule 2). Labeling is a prerequisite for other items, not a decision of its own; vendors are already shipping titles natively so this is commodity.

actionThatDiffers: Instead of pasting the review request into the workflow gate yourself, it arrives routed. Same review, one fewer paste.
why: Doing it today is typing one prompt into the Spacedock skill, which is the 21-40 band (rule 5). Impact is capped by audience: it only pays off for the small set of users already running Spacedock workflows, and for them it removes a copy-paste rather than changing a decision.

actionThatDiffers: You add a deny rule or a confirmation gate for the class of action that just fired, and you revert the specific damage while it is still revertible, instead of discovering a force-push or a dropped table days later.
why: Destructive tool calls scroll out of the visible pane, so a capture-pane sweep does not recover them; you would be grepping transcripts across sessions and time, which most users will not do (61-80). Nothing anywhere computes irreversibility, so the value rests on a heuristic classifier being right, hence dependsOnDetector. Impact is real but post-hoc: it reports after the fact, and the follow-up action (tighten permissions) is one people already take reactively when they happen to notice.

actionThatDiffers: You reprioritise which session to attend to, and occasionally spot two sessions duplicating the same work. Mostly a nicer label than D2.
why: The originating prompt is the first thing in every pane and in every harness session file, so a one-pass sweep gives an adequate approximation of goal-per-session (rule 2). The outcome word is steering, which is not an action; the concrete action I can name is weak reprioritisation, so impact stays at or below 50 per rule 1.

actionThatDiffers: You go straight to the session that needs you rather than round-robin sampling tabs, so an agent that finished or blocked gets picked up in a minute instead of ten.
why: No harness shows other sessions, but enumeration specifically is what the six-line loop is good at: tmux list-panes plus ps names every running session, and cycling tabs works at 3-12 sessions. That is approximate-but-adequate, so rule 2 caps access. Impact is genuine and recurring at this session count, and no single vendor can ship the cross-harness version, which limits the commodity risk. Held under 76 because the loss avoided is diffuse idle-agent minutes, not a blown window.

actionThatDiffers: Almost nothing. Model is chosen at session start; nobody restarts a running session to downgrade it mid-turn.
why: The model is on the Claude Code status line and the Codex usage line unprompted, so per-pane it is already on screen and the cross-session view is arithmetic aggregation of individually visible fields (rules 2 and 3). The stated outcome, moving cheap work off the expensive model, requires abandoning and restarting a session, which is exactly the action users decline to take. Interesting, no action follows.

actionThatDiffers: With quota near the wall you stop the highest-burn session specifically, rather than stopping several or letting the window blow.
why: Per-session token consumption rate is nowhere native and needs transcript deltas over a window, but pane verbosity is a usable proxy in one sweep, so this lands at the top of reachable rather than above it. No tool computes the number, so the value rests on the rate heuristic being accurate. Impact is attacked hard: burn rate answers which session is expensive, not which is expendable, and the kill decision is a value judgement it does not supply. It also only matters in the narrow window where quota is tight.

actionThatDiffers: None outside the tool. You clear a row. The agents, repos and quota are unaffected.
why: Kind is action: it is a click, and clicking one existing affordance sits in the 21-40 band (rule 5). Impact is pure tool hygiene and entirely conditional on other items existing first. It keeps a board trustworthy, which is second-order product plumbing, not a user decision. Under rule 1 there is no concrete external action, so it stays low.

actionThatDiffers: You start the next task in Codex or Gemini before the Claude window is exhausted, instead of discovering the wall mid-task and switching then.
why: Two of the harnesses hand you a current figure for one command (Claude /usage, the Codex usage line) and Barista caches Claude without asking, so the honest reading is visiting several places, the 41-60 band, nudged to the top because several harnesses expose no quota at all. Impact is the strongest of my nine because the action is one users already perform, but that is also the attack: they perform it reactively when the harness blocks them, and reactive switching is nearly as good. The delta is roughly twenty minutes of foresight, not a prevented loss, so it does not reach 76.
